quick.summary: Why surprising a room full of leaders with a massive change always fails.
quick.takeaway: Show your plan to key stakeholders in private before the official meeting.

beats.line: My architecture pitch got killed instantly. Why was the engineering lead so mad?
Imagine throwing a massive surprise party for someone who hates surprises.
It would be a total disaster. They would walk right out.
Exactly. Big technical changes are just like that. Nobody likes a surprise.
Leaders need time to process before the big meeting even starts.
You failed to build a stakeholder coalition.
Can I just say get them on board early?
Yes. Show them the plan one on one, a week before.
So I ask for their thoughts in private before the official pitch.
That is how you turn an enemy into a sponsor.

quiz.question: You have a major architectural change to propose at Thursday's meeting. What should you do on Monday?
options: Run through the slides with your dog.
Send a surprise email to the whole team.
Show the plan to the key leaders privately.
Refuse to answer any questions until Thursday.
quiz.explanation: Key leaders need to see the proposal beforehand so they are not surprised in front of their peers.

quiz.question: Surprising a leader with a bold new idea in a large meeting is a good way to win them over.
quiz.explanation: Surprises almost always result in immediate pushback. Give leaders time to process your idea privately.
